before: Jerusalem was destroyed by Babylon in the early sixth century BC. Under Persia, exiles returned (notably under Cyrus, about 538 BC) and the temple was rebuilt, but the city walls stayed broken. An earlier report of this ruin reached Nehemiah (Neh 1), moving him to mourn, fast, and pray. A prior imperial order had even stopped rebuilding work by force (Ezra 4:17–23) — the backdrop that makes his new request dangerous.

entities.extended_description: A Jewish official serving in the Persian royal court during the reign of Artaxerxes I. After receiving a troubling report about Jerusalem, he sought and received royal permission to travel there and lead the rebuilding of its walls, afterwards serving as governor of Judah.
entities.short_description: Jewish cupbearer to Artaxerxes I who sought permission to rebuild Jerusalem's walls.

entities.extended_description: A king of the Persian Achaemenid Empire who ruled in the fifth century BC (commonly dated approximately 465–424 BC; exact regnal-year reckoning varies by source and must be confirmed by the reviewer). The province of Judah was under his empire's administration during Nehemiah's time.
entities.short_description: Persian king in the fifth century BC whose empire governed Judah in Nehemiah's time.

entities.extended_description: A major administrative center of the Persian Empire, traditionally associated with the royal court where Nehemiah served (see Neh 1:1). The identification of the Nehemiah 2 court scene with Susa rests on that association, not on a city name in chapter 2 itself.
entities.short_description: Major Persian administrative center traditionally associated with Nehemiah's court service.

entities.extended_description: The historic city of Judah, destroyed by Babylon in the early sixth century BC and partly resettled after the Persian conquest of Babylon. In Nehemiah 2 its temple has been rebuilt but its walls and gates remain in ruins, leaving it vulnerable and disgraced.
entities.short_description: Historic city of Judah whose walls and gates lay in ruins in Nehemiah's time.

entities.extended_description: The empire that conquered Babylon and governed Judah through provinces such as Beyond the River. Royal permission, official letters, and military escort in Nehemiah 2 reflect how movement and building projects depended on imperial authority.
entities.short_description: The empire governing Judah in Nehemiah's time; its permission and resources drive this chapter.

entities.extended_description: A trusted court office involving close, regular access to the king — in Nehemiah's case, serving wine. That access explains both his opportunity to speak and the danger of appearing sad in the royal presence.
entities.short_description: Trusted court office with close access to the king; Nehemiah's position in this chapter.

entities.extended_description: Named in Nehemiah 2:8 as the keeper of the king's forest from whom Nehemiah requests timber. Nothing else in the chapter identifies him further; reviewers should confirm whether any other source adds reliable detail.
entities.short_description: Keeper of the royal forest named as a source of timber for the rebuilding.

entities.extended_description: A regional opponent of the rebuilding effort, introduced in Nehemiah 2:10 alongside Tobiah and later Geshem. The chapter presents him as deeply disturbed by Nehemiah's mission and later as one who mocks it.
entities.short_description: Regional opponent deeply disturbed by Nehemiah's mission to Jerusalem.

entities.extended_description: An Ammonite official who, with Sanballat, opposes Nehemiah's mission from its arrival. The chapter gives his title and reaction but little else; further detail needs reviewer-confirmed sources.
entities.short_description: Ammonite official who opposes Nehemiah's mission alongside Sanballat.

entities.extended_description: Named in Nehemiah 2:19 with Sanballat and Tobiah among those who mock the rebuilding plan. The chapter gives no further detail; reviewers should confirm any additional identification.
entities.short_description: Arabian figure named among those who mock the rebuilding plan.

entities.extended_description: The homeland region and Persian-administered area containing Jerusalem, named in Nehemiah's request as his destination. Travel there required passing through the province Beyond the River.
entities.short_description: Homeland region containing Jerusalem; Nehemiah's requested destination.

entities.extended_description: The Persian administrative region west of the Euphrates through which Nehemiah must travel. His request for letters to its governors shows that safe passage depended on imperial authorization.
entities.short_description: Persian region west of the Euphrates whose governors control Nehemiah's route.

entities.extended_description: A Jerusalem gate named as the start and end point of Nehemiah's night inspection (Neh 2:13, 15). Its exact Persian-period location is reconstructed from excavation and later texts; reviewers must confirm the map placement and its uncertainty note.
entities.short_description: Jerusalem gate marking the start and end of the night inspection route.

entities.extended_description: A water feature named in Nehemiah 2:14 on the inspection route, near the Fountain Gate. Traditional associations exist, but the exact identification needs reviewer-confirmed sources and a visible uncertainty label.
entities.short_description: Water feature on the night inspection route near the Fountain Gate.

entities.extended_description: In Nehemiah 2:4 the king asks what Nehemiah wants, and the chapter records that he prayed to the God of heaven before answering. No wording is given in the chapter; reviewers should confirm any further detail.
entities.short_description: Nehemiah's brief prayer to the God of heaven before answering Artaxerxes.

entities.extended_description: In Nehemiah 2:7–8 Nehemiah asks the king for letters to the governors Beyond the River and to Asaph, keeper of the royal forest; in 2:9 he delivers the king's letters. No wording is recorded in the chapter; reviewers should confirm any further detail.
entities.short_description: Written orders from Artaxerxes carried by Nehemiah for passage and timber.

immediate_summary: Nehemiah, a Jewish cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I, receives permission, letters, timber, and an escort to rebuild Jerusalem's ruined walls; after arriving he secretly inspects the damage at night, rallies the people, and faces mockery from regional opponents.

stakes: Nehemiah needs imperial permission, protected travel, and materials; appearing sad before the king is personally dangerous, and asking the king to reverse the earlier stop-work order (see Ezra 4:17–23) is politically dangerous. For Jerusalem, walls mean security, trade, and civic dignity; rebuilding them will provoke the organized opposition introduced at the chapter's edges.

the_moment.text: Nehemiah stands before the Persian king, who has noticed his sadness. He has one opportunity to ask permission to rebuild Jerusalem — so he first prays to the God of heaven.

what: The king notices Nehemiah's sadness. Nehemiah, afraid, prays and asks to be sent to Judah with letters for safe passage and timber for the gates, wall, and a house. The request is granted. He travels with an escort, meets grieving opposition, reaches Jerusalem, secretly inspects the broken walls by night, rallies the people, and answers mockery with confidence in God.
when: Nisan (roughly March/April) in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes — commonly rendered about 445 BC. Label as approximate: ancient regnal-year reckoning varies between sources.
where: The Persian royal court (traditionally associated with Susa; chapter 2 itself names no city, so keep the association labeled), then the road through Beyond the River to Jerusalem and Judah.
who: Nehemiah, a Jewish cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I; the king, who notices his sadness and grants the request; the queen, present at the exchange; later Asaph (timber), the governors Beyond the River (letters), and the opponents Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem.
